**Problem A1: Shake It**
Most hairy mammals shake after getting wet; shaking the water off is energetically advantageous to waiting for it to dry on its own. In this problem, we investigate the mechanics of shaking off water. For simplicity, we will model animals as solid cylinders with the sides covered in fur. You may ignore gravity throughout the problem.

a. We can model the shaking by assuming that the angular position of the cylinder undergoes a sinusoidal oscillation: θ = A cos(ωt). (The rotation is about the axis of rotational symmetry.) Letting the radius of the cylindrical animal be R, derive an expression for the magnitude of the acceleration of a point on the surface of the animal under such a motion.

b. For the rest of this problem, rather than modeling sinusoidal motion, we will assume that the cylindrical animal is simply spinning at constant angular speed ω. Wet fur tends to separate into cylindrical clumps of radius r ≪ R. A droplet of water on the end of a clump of fur will be separated from it if the centripetal force overcomes the forces due to surface tension. Derive an approximate relationship (valid up to scalar numerical constants) between the surface tension σ, the radius r of the fur clump, the radius R of the animal, the angular speed ω, and the density ρ of water. The diagram below show the cross-section of the animal, showing four clumps of fur with droplets on their end.
[Diagram description: A large circle representing the cross-section of the cylindrical animal. On the right side of the circle, four small, closely spaced cylindrical clumps of fur protrude radially outward. Each clump has a small hemispherical droplet of water at its outer end.]

c. Experimentally, it is observed that all mammalian fur forms clumps of similar radius. Under the assumption that different animals all have the same density and are simply scaled copies of each other (i.e. larger animals are both longer and fatter), the relationship between an animal’s mass M and its angular velocity of shaking ω is of the form ω ∼ M^n: find the value of n.

d. Shaking requires energy, which we can crudely model as the rotational energy of the corresponding cylinder. An alternative strategy for the animal is to simply air-dry their fur, which requires energy to evaporate the water. Assume a wet animal has approximately 5% of their body weight in water, and has to supply all the energy for evaporating the water. Our model predicts that for some animal sizes, it will be energetically advantageous to air dry themselves: estimate the range of animal masses for which this is true. You may use the following facts: a mouse weighs 20 g, has a radius of 1 cm, and shakes itself with angular velocity ω = 30 rad/s. The latent heat of vaporization of water at room temperature is λ = 2430 J/g.

**Part a**
The angular position of a point on the surface of the cylinder is given by $\theta = A \cos(\omega t)$. The linear position of this point along the tangent to the cylinder's surface is $x = R \theta = R A \cos(\omega t)$. 
The tangential velocity of the point is:
$$v = \dot{x} = -R A \omega \sin(\omega t)$$
The tangential acceleration is:
$$a_t = \dot{v} = -R A \omega^2 \cos(\omega t)$$
The centripetal acceleration is:
$$a_c = \frac{v^2}{R} = R A^2 \omega^2 \sin^2(\omega t)$$
The magnitude of the total acceleration is the vector sum of the tangential and centripetal components:
$$a = \sqrt{a_t^2 + a_c^2} = \sqrt{R^2 A^2 \omega^4 \cos^2(\omega t) + R^2 A^4 \omega^4 \sin^2(\omega t)}$$
$$a = R A \omega^2 \sqrt{\cos^2(\omega t) + A^2 \sin^2(\omega t)}$$

**Part b**
The droplet of water at the end of a clump of fur is approximately hemispherical with radius $r$. The volume of the droplet is $V \approx \frac{2}{3}\pi r^3 \sim r^3$, and its mass is $m \approx \rho r^3$. The droplet is located at a distance $R + r \approx R$ (since $r \ll R$) from the axis of rotation.
The centripetal force required to keep the droplet moving in a circle is:
$$F_c = m \omega^2 R \approx \rho r^3 \omega^2 R$$
The force holding the droplet to the fur clump is due to surface tension, which acts along the perimeter of the base of the hemispherical droplet (a circle of radius $r$). The length of this contact line is $2\pi r$, so the surface tension force is:
$$F_\sigma = \sigma \times (2\pi r) \sim \sigma r$$
For the droplet to be separated from the fur, the centripetal force must overcome the surface tension force ($F_c \approx F_\sigma$):
$$\rho r^3 \omega^2 R \approx \sigma r$$
Dividing both sides by $r$, we obtain the approximate relationship:
$$\rho r^2 \omega^2 R \approx \sigma$$

**Part c**
From the relationship derived in part (b), $\rho r^2 \omega^2 R \approx \sigma$. Since all mammalian fur forms clumps of similar radius, $r$ is a constant. The surface tension $\sigma$ and water density $\rho$ are also constants. Thus:
$$\omega^2 R \approx \text{constant} \implies \omega^2 \propto R^{-1}$$
Assuming animals have the same density and are scaled copies of each other, their mass scales with their volume: $M \propto R^3$, which means $R \propto M^{1/3}$. Substituting this into the proportionality for $\omega$:
$$\omega^2 \propto (M^{1/3})^{-1} = M^{-1/3}$$
$$\omega \propto M^{-1/6}$$
Thus, the value of $n$ is **$-1/6$**.

**Part d**
The rotational kinetic energy of the solid cylindrical animal is given by:
$$E_{shake} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2 = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{1}{2} M R^2\right) \omega^2 = \frac{1}{4} M R^2 \omega^2$$
Using the scaling relations $R \propto M^{1/3}$ and $\omega \propto M^{-1/6}$, the shaking energy scales as:
$$E_{shake} \propto M \cdot M^{2/3} \cdot M^{-1/3} = M^{4/3}$$
The energy required to air-dry by evaporating the water is proportional to the mass of the water on the animal:
$$E_{evap} = 0.05 M \lambda \propto M$$
Air-drying becomes energetically advantageous when $E_{shake} > E_{evap}$, which occurs for sufficiently large masses since $E_{shake}$ grows faster ($M^{4/3}$) than $E_{evap}$ ($M$).
Setting $E_{shake} = E_{evap}$ to find the threshold mass $M_{thresh}$:
$$\frac{1}{4} M_{thresh} R_{thresh}^2 \omega_{thresh}^2 = 0.05 M_{thresh} \lambda$$
$$R_{thresh}^2 \omega_{thresh}^2 = 0.2 \lambda$$
Using the scaling $R^2 \omega^2 \propto M^{1/3}$, we can relate the threshold mass to the mouse's parameters:
$$\left(\frac{M_{thresh}}{M_{mouse}}\right)^{1/3} = \frac{0.2 \lambda}{R_{mouse}^2 \omega_{mouse}^2}$$
Substituting the given values ($\lambda = 2430$ J/g $= 2.43 \times 10^6$ J/kg, $R_{mouse} = 0.01$ m, $\omega_{mouse} = 30$ rad/s, $M_{mouse} = 0.02$ kg):
$$\frac{0.2 \lambda}{R_{mouse}^2 \omega_{mouse}^2} = \frac{0.2 \times 2.43 \times 10^6}{(0.01)^2 \times (30)^2} = \frac{486000}{0.09} = 5.4 \times 10^6$$
$$M_{thresh} = M_{mouse} \times (5.4 \times 10^6)^3 = 0.02 \text{ kg} \times 1.57 \times 10^{20} \approx 3.1 \times 10^{18} \text{ kg}$$
Thus, it is energetically advantageous to air dry for animal masses greater than this threshold.

**Final Answers:**
a. $a = R A \omega^2 \sqrt{\cos^2(\omega t) + A^2 \sin^2(\omega t)}$
b. $\rho r^2 \omega^2 R \sim \sigma$
c. $n = -1/6$
d. $M > 3 \times 10^{18}$ kg

Problem A2: Black Tides

Consider a spherically symmetric, nonrotating star of mass $m$ and radius $r$. If it gets too close to the supermassive black hole of mass $M \gg m$ at the center of a galaxy, it will be ripped apart by tidal forces. Throughout this problem, neglect relativistic effects and give answers in terms of $G$, $M$, $m$, and $r$. When asked for numbers, assume the star is Sun-like, so that $m = 2 \times 10^{30} \text{ kg}$, $r = 7 \times 10^8 \text{ m}$, and $M = 10^6 m$, and give all numeric answers to one significant figure.

a. Suppose the star orbits the black hole in a circle of radius $R$. What is the radius of curvature of the trajectory of each point on the star's surface? Note that the star does not rotate as it orbits.

b. Gas on the star's surface facing the black hole is attracted to the star by the star's gravity, and pulled away from the star by the black hole's tidal force. Write an expression for the tidal acceleration at the point closest to the black hole.

c. At a radius $R$ where the gravitational and tidal forces are in equilibrium, the star will start being tidally ripped apart. This effect can only be observed when $R$ is outside the black hole's Schwarzschild radius $R_s = 2GM/c^2$. Find an expression for $R$ and numerically evaluate the ratio $R/R_s$.

For the rest of the problem, we consider a star on a parabolic orbit whose periapsis (distance of closest approach) is equal to the radius $R$ found in part c. Near periapsis, the star will be torn apart in a “tidal disruption event”. As a very rough model of this phenomenon, assume the star is initially a single rigid body. The moment it reaches periapsis, it fragments into many rigid pieces which do not interact with other, and feel only the black hole's gravity.

d. Afterward, some of the fragments will escape from the black hole, while the rest remain bound. Numerically evaluate the fraction of the mass which escapes.

e. An escaping fragment has speed $v_f$ when it is far from the black hole. Find the maximum possible value of $v_f$, among all fragments, and evaluate it numerically.

f. A bound fragment orbits with period $T_f$. Find the minimum possible value of $T_f$, among all fragments, and evaluate it numerically.

As bound fragments return to the location of the initial disruption, they collide with other debris, causing them to be absorbed into the black hole's accretion disk. This process produces an enormous amount of light, with the luminosity (or energy emitted over time) proportional to the mass absorption rate. If $t = 0$ at the moment the star fragments apart, then light begins to be emitted at the time you found in part f, and afterward the luminosity scales as $L \propto 1/t^n$ for a constant $n$.

g. Find the value of $n$. Assume for simplicity that the total energies of the bound fragments are uniformly distributed between their minimum and maximum values.
turns.official_answer:
a. $R$
b. $\frac{2GMr}{R^3}$
c. $R = r\left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/3}$, $R/R_s = 30$
d. $0.5$
e. $v_f = \left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/6} \sqrt{\frac{Gm}{r}} = 5 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}$
f. $T_f = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{r^3}{2Gm}} \sqrt{\frac{M}{m}} = 7 \times 10^6 \text{ s} = 80 \text{ days}$
g. $n = 5/3$

**Part a**
Since the star does not rotate as it orbits, its orientation remains fixed in the inertial frame. This means that the velocity and acceleration of every point on the star are identical to the velocity and acceleration of the center of mass. The trajectory of any point on the star is simply the trajectory of the center of mass (a circle of radius $R$) shifted by a constant vector. Since the path of every point is a circle of radius $R$, the radius of curvature for each point on the star's surface is:
$$\rho = R$$

**Part b**
The tidal acceleration at the point closest to the black hole is the difference between the gravitational acceleration at that point and the gravitational acceleration at the center of mass. The closest point is at a distance $R - r$ from the black hole.
$$a_{tidal} = \frac{GM}{(R-r)^2} - \frac{GM}{R^2}$$
Factoring out $GM/R^2$ and expanding for $r \ll R$:
$$a_{tidal} = \frac{GM}{R^2} \left[ \left(1 - \frac{r}{R}\right)^{-2} - 1 \right] \approx \frac{GM}{R^2} \left( 1 + 2\frac{r}{R} - 1 \right) = \frac{2GMr}{R^3}$$

**Part c**
The star begins to be ripped apart when the tidal acceleration pulling the surface gas away equals the star's gravitational acceleration holding it in:
$$\frac{2GMr}{R^3} = \frac{Gm}{r^2}$$
Solving for $R$, we get:
$$R^3 = \frac{2M}{m}r^3 \implies R = r \left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/3}$$
To find the ratio $R/R_s$, we use the Schwarzschild radius $R_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2}$. Plugging in the given values $m = 2 \times 10^{30} \text{ kg}$, $r = 7 \times 10^8 \text{ m}$, and $M = 10^6 m = 2 \times 10^{36} \text{ kg}$:
$$R = 7 \times 10^8 \left(\frac{2 \times 2 \times 10^{36}}{2 \times 10^{30}}\right)^{1/3} = 7 \times 10^8 \times (2 \times 10^6)^{1/3} \approx 8.82 \times 10^{10} \text{ m}$$
$$R_s = \frac{2(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(2 \times 10^{36})}{(3 \times 10^8)^2} \approx 2.96 \times 10^9 \text{ m}$$
$$\frac{R}{R_s} = \frac{8.82 \times 10^{10}}{2.96 \times 10^9} \approx 29.8$$
To one significant figure, this ratio is **30**.

**Part d**
At the moment the star fragments, it is at periapsis of its parabolic orbit, so the center of mass velocity is $v_{CM} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$. Since it was a rigid body, all fragments initially share this velocity $v_{CM}$. The specific energy of a fragment at distance $d$ from the black hole is:
$$E = \frac{1}{2}v_{CM}^2 - \frac{GM}{d} = \frac{GM}{R} - \frac{GM}{d}$$
A fragment escapes if its energy is non-negative ($E \ge 0$), which occurs when $d \ge R$. Because the star is a sphere of radius $r$ centered at distance $R$, the plane $d = R$ slices exactly through the center of the star, dividing it into two equal hemispheres. Thus, the fraction of the mass which escapes is:
**0.5**

**Part e**
The maximum speed $v_f$ at infinity corresponds to the fragment with the maximum energy, which is the fragment at the farthest point from the black hole, $d = R + r$. 
$$E_{max} = \frac{GM}{R} - \frac{GM}{R+r} = \frac{GMr}{R(R+r)} \approx \frac{GMr}{R^2}$$
Setting $E_{max} = \frac{1}{2}v_f^2$, we find:
$$v_f = \sqrt{\frac{2GMr}{R^2}}$$
Substituting $R \approx 8.82 \times 10^{10}$ m:
$$v_f = \sqrt{\frac{2(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(2 \times 10^{36})(7 \times 10^8)}{(8.82 \times 10^{10})^2}} \approx 4.9 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}$$
To one significant figure, the maximum speed is **$5 \times 10^6$ m/s**.

**Part f**
The minimum period corresponds to the most tightly bound fragment, which is at $d = R - r$. Its specific energy is $E_{min} = -\frac{GMr}{R(R-r)} \approx -\frac{GMr}{R^2}$. The semi-major axis $a$ of its orbit is given by $E = -\frac{GM}{2a}$, yielding:
$$a = \frac{R^2}{2r}$$
By Kepler's Third Law, the period is $T_f = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{a^3}{GM}}$. Substituting $a$:
$$T_f = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{R^6}{8GMr^3}} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi^2 R^6}{2GMr^3}}$$
Using $R = r(2M/m)^{1/3}$, this simplifies to $T_f = \sqrt{\frac{2\pi^2 r^3 M}{Gm^2}}$. Numerically:
$$T_f = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{(5.56 \times 10^{12})^3}{(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(2 \times 10^{36})}} \approx 7.1 \times 10^6 \text{ s}$$
To one significant figure, the minimum period is **$7 \times 10^6$ s** (or about 80 days).

**Part g**
The bound fragments have specific energies uniformly distributed between $E_{min}$ and $0$, so $dn \propto dE$. The period of a fragment is $T \propto a^{3/2} \propto (-E)^{-3/2}$, which implies $E \propto -T^{-2/3}$.
Differentiating gives the number of fragments returning per unit time:
$$\left|\frac{dN}{dT}\right| \propto \left|\frac{dE}{dT}\right| \propto \frac{2}{3}T^{-5/3}$$
Since fragments return at time $t = T$ and the luminosity is proportional to the mass return rate, we have:
$$L \propto \frac{dM}{dt} \propto t^{-5/3}$$
Comparing this to $L \propto 1/t^n$, we find:
**$n = 5/3$**

In this problem, we explore some of the design considerations for an electromagnet.

**a.** Consider an electromagnet consisting of a long solenoid, i.e. a spiral of thin wire wrapped in a single layer around a cylindrical nonmagnetic core. The wire is wrapped in such a way that the adjacent coils almost touch. When a current is sent through the wire, a magnetic field is generated inside the solenoid; this magnetic field exerts an outward force on the wire. Find the pressure $P$ on the solenoid in terms of the magnetic field $B$ inside the solenoid.

**b.** The pressure on the "walls" of the solenoid is counteracted by tension inside the wire. Derive an expression for the maximal achievable magnetic field $B$ in terms of coil radius $a$, wire diameter (thickness) $t \ll a$, and wire tensile strength $\sigma$. (The tensile strength of a material is the force per unit cross-sectional area that needs to be applied in order to pull the material apart.) Assume the wire is circular in cross-section.

**c.** Let $a = 0.1\text{ m}$, $t = 0.001\text{ m}$. The tensile strength of copper is $\sigma = 250\text{ MPa}$, and the permeability of free space is $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ H/m}$. What is the maximum magnetic field that can be achieved in a single-layer solenoid made out of such a wire without the wire snapping?

**d.** In theory, we could generate a stronger field by increasing the wire thickness, but the nonuniform distribution of current inside the wire makes this difficult to analyze.
Instead, consider wrapping the solenoid in many layers of wire. We will place adjacent layers a distance $t$ apart so that they just barely don't touch, and will adjust the current through each wire to equalize the tensile stress. The wire coils span the space from an inner core radius of $a$ to an outer radius of $b$. Estimate the maximum achievable field strength inside this electromagnet. You may assume that the wire is thin ($t \ll a$, $t \ll b - a$).

**e.** Estimate the numeric value of the maximum magnetic field that can be achieved in a multi-layer solenoid described above with $a = 0.1\text{ m}$ and $b = 0.3\text{ m}$.

Consider a disk with mass $m$ and radius $R$ placed on a large and frictionless table. An ant with mass $m$ is placed on top of the disk. The ant can move freely without sliding on the disk.

a. Initially, the ant starts on the edge of the disk, and both the ant and the disk are at rest (relative to the table). c. Now there are two ants on the disk! The second ant (also of mass $m$) starts at distance $R/2$ from the center of the disk, with an angle offset by $\theta$ from the first ant. The second ant walks counterclockwise around this circle with radius $R/2$ at speed $v/2$ (relative to the disk). Find all $\theta$ such that the second ant is stationary in the frame of the table.

turns.candidate_answer:
**Part a**
Let the velocity of the disk's center in the table frame be $V_D$ and the velocity of the ant be $V_A$. Since the table is frictionless, there are no external horizontal forces, so the total linear momentum of the system is conserved. Initially, both are at rest, so the center of mass remains stationary:
$$m V_D + m V_A = 0 \implies V_D = -V_A$$
The ant's velocity relative to the disk is $v$ in the direction of the diameter (let's call this the $x$-direction). Thus:
$$V_A = V_D + v \hat{x}$$
Substituting $V_D = -V_A$ into the equation above:
$$V_A = -V_A + v \hat{x} \implies 2V_A = v \hat{x} \implies V_A = \frac{v}{2} \hat{x}$$
Since the ant moves along the diameter, it exerts no torque on the disk about its center, so the disk does not rotate ($\omega = 0$). The ant's velocity in the frame of the table is **$v/2$** in the direction of its motion.

**Part b**
Now the ant walks counterclockwise along the edge of the disk at constant speed $v$ relative to the disk. Let the angular velocity of the disk be $\omega$. The ant's velocity in the table frame is:
$$V_A = V_D + \omega R \hat{\theta} + v \hat{\theta}$$
Using conservation of linear momentum ($V_D = -V_A$):
$$-V_D = V_D + (\omega R + v)\hat{\theta} \implies V_D = -\frac{1}{2}(\omega R + v)\hat{\theta}$$
To find $\omega$, we use conservation of angular momentum about the center of mass. The center of mass is located halfway between the disk center and the ant, so $R_{D/cm} = -\frac{R}{2}\hat{r}$ and $R_{A/cm} = \frac{R}{2}\hat{r}$. The total angular momentum is:
$$L_{cm} = I_D \omega + m R_{D/cm} \times V_D + m R_{A/cm} \times V_A = 0$$
Since $V_A = -V_D$, the cross products add up:
$$L_{cm} = \frac{1}{2}mR^2\omega + m\left(\frac{R}{2}\hat{r}\right) \times V_A + m\left(-\frac{R}{2}\hat{r}\right) \times (-V_A) = \frac{1}{2}mR^2\omega + mR\hat{r} \times V_A = 0$$
Substituting $V_A = \frac{1}{2}(\omega R + v)\hat{\theta}$ and $\hat{r} \times \hat{\theta} = \hat{z}$:
$$\frac{1}{2}mR^2\omega + mR\left(\frac{1}{2}(\omega R + v)\right) = 0$$
$$\frac{1}{2}R\omega + \frac{1}{2}\omega R + \frac{1}{2}v = 0 \implies R\omega + \frac{v}{2} = 0 \implies \omega = -\frac{v}{2R}$$
Now we can find the ant's speed in the table frame:
$$V_A = \frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{v}{2R}R + v\right)\hat{\theta} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{v}{2}\right)\hat{\theta} = \frac{v}{4}\hat{\theta}$$
The ant's speed in the frame of the table is **$v/4$**.

**Part c**
For two ants, let $V_1$ and $V_2$ be their velocities in the table frame, and $V_D$ be the disk's velocity. Conservation of linear momentum gives:
$$m V_D + m V_1 + m V_2 = 0$$
We want the second ant to be stationary in the table frame, so $V_2 = 0$. This yields $V_1 = -V_D$.
The velocity of Ant 1 in the table frame is:
$$V_1 = V_D + (\omega R + v)\hat{\theta}_1$$
Substituting $V_1 = -V_D$:
$$-V_D = V_D + (\omega R + v)\hat{\theta}_1 \implies V_D = -\frac{1}{2}(\omega R + v)\hat{\theta}_1$$
The velocity of Ant 2 in the table frame is:
$$V_2 = V_D + \left(\omega \frac{R}{2} + \frac{v}{2}\right)\hat{\theta}_2 = 0$$
$$V_D = -\frac{1}{2}(\omega R + v)\hat{\theta}_2$$
Equating the two expressions for $V_D$:
$$-\frac{1}{2}(\omega R + v)\hat{\theta}_1 = -\frac{1}{2}(\omega R + v)\hat{\theta}_2$$
Assuming $\omega R + v \neq 0$ (if it were 0, $V_D = 0$ and $V_1 = 0$, which would violate angular momentum conservation as $L = I_D\omega \neq 0$), we must have:
$$\hat{\theta}_1 = \hat{\theta}_2$$
For the tangential unit vectors of the two ants to be identical, their radial position vectors must also point in the same direction, which means the angle offset between them must be zero.
Let's verify this with angular momentum conservation. If $\theta = 0$, then Ant 2 is at $R/2$ on the same radial line as Ant 1. The center of mass of the system is exactly at Ant 2's position. Because $V_2 = 0$, the center of mass is stationary, which is consistent. The angular momentum about the center of mass (Ant 2) must be zero:
$$L_{cm} = I_D \omega + m R_{D/cm} \times V_D + m R_{1/cm} \times V_1 = 0$$
With $\theta = 0$, $R_{D/cm} = -\frac{R}{2}\hat{r}$ and $R_{1/cm} = \frac{R}{2}\hat{r}$, which yields the exact same angular momentum equation as in Part b, giving $\omega = -v/(2R)$ and $V_D = -v/4\hat{\theta}$. This confirms the kinematics perfectly match the prescribed relative velocities of both ants. 
Thus, the only angle offset that works is **$0$**.

Problem B2: Where's the Kaboom?

A plane is flying horizontally at constant velocity $v$ and altitude $z = H$. The speed of sound at altitude $z$ is given by
$$c(z) = \alpha \sqrt{T(z)},$$
where $\alpha$ is a constant. Suppose $v > c(H)$, and define the Mach number as
$$M \equiv \frac{v}{c(H)} > 1.$$
If $c(z)$ is constant for all $z$, then the envelope is a cone with half angle $\theta$ where $\sin \theta = \frac{1}{M}$ and propagates with the speed of sound $c$.

a. Sketch the envelope.

b. Now, the speed of sound depends on the altitude because the temperature is not uniform. For the altitudes we are interested in, the following linear model works well:
$$T(z) = T_0 - \beta z,$$
where $\beta > 0$ is a constant. Sketch the envelope of the boom.

c. If the Mach number is large enough then the sonic boom hits the ground. Assume it is large enough. On the ground, there are two sensors at $z = 0$ and $z = h$, one directly above the other. Assume $h \ll H$ and $\beta h \ll T_0$. At time $t_1$, the top sensor receives the sonic boom signal and at a later time, the bottom sensor also receives the signal. Express the Mach number $M$ of the airplane in terms of $H, h, t, T_0, \alpha, \beta$, where $t = t_2 - t_1$.

d. If the plane travels slower without changing direction, its sonic boom could become no longer audible from the ground for the Mach number $1 < M < M_{\text{max}}$. What is the upper limit for the Mach number $M_{\text{max}}$ for which this can occur? Express your answer in terms of $T_0, H, \alpha, \beta$. You do not necessarily need all of these parameters.

c. $M = \left[ \left(1 - \frac{\beta H}{T_0}\right) \left(1 - \frac{\alpha^2 t^2 T_0}{h^2}\right) \right]^{-1/2}$

d. $M_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{T_0}{T_0 - \beta H}}$

**Part a**
The envelope of the sonic boom is a right circular cone with its apex at the airplane. The cone opens backwards in the direction opposite to the plane's motion. The axis of the cone is the trajectory of the plane, and the half-angle $\theta$ between the surface of the cone and the horizontal trajectory satisfies $\sin\theta = \frac{1}{M} = \frac{c(H)}{v}$.

**Part b**
Since the temperature decreases with altitude ($T(z) = T_0 - \beta z$), the speed of sound $c(z) = \alpha\sqrt{T(z)}$ also decreases with altitude. As the acoustic rays travel downwards into regions of higher sound speed, Snell's law dictates that they bend towards the horizontal (the angle of the rays with the vertical increases). Consequently, the wavefront (which is perpendicular to the rays) curves outwards, away from the vertical axis. The sketch of the envelope is a curved surface resembling a horn or trumpet that opens up wider than the cone in part (a), curving away from the vertical as it extends downwards towards the ground.

**Part c**
The sonic boom wavefront is a surface of constant phase. Because the source moves at a constant horizontal velocity $v$ and the medium only depends on $z$, the wavefront pattern moves horizontally at velocity $v$. We can transform to the frame moving with the plane by letting $\xi = x - vt$. The wavefront in this frame is stationary and satisfies the eikonal equation for the transformed wave equation. This yields the shape of the wavefront as:
$$ \xi = -\int_H^z \frac{\sqrt{v^2 - c(z')^2}}{c(z')} dz' $$
The vertical velocity of the wavefront along a vertical line $x = \text{const}$ is found by differentiating $x - vt = \xi(z)$ with respect to $t$:
$$ -v = -\frac{\sqrt{v^2 - c(z)^2}}{c(z)} \frac{dz}{dt} \implies v_z(z) = \frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{v c(z)}{\sqrt{v^2 - c(z)^2}} $$
The time difference between the top and bottom sensors is the time it takes for the wavefront to travel from $z=h$ to $z=0$:
$$ t = \int_0^h \frac{dz}{v_z(z)} = \int_0^h \frac{\sqrt{v^2 - c(z)^2}}{v c(z)} dz $$
Since $h \ll H$ and $\beta h \ll T_0$, the speed of sound is approximately constant over this small interval, $c(z) \approx c(0) = \alpha\sqrt{T_0} \equiv c_0$. The integral simplifies to:
$$ t \approx \frac{h \sqrt{v^2 - c_0^2}}{v c_0} $$
Solving for the plane's velocity $v$:
$$ v c_0 t = h \sqrt{v^2 - c_0^2} \implies v^2 c_0^2 t^2 = h^2 v^2 - h^2 c_0^2 \implies v^2 = \frac{h^2 c_0^2}{c_0^2 t^2 - h^2} $$
The Mach number is $M = \frac{v}{c(H)} = \frac{v}{\alpha\sqrt{T_0 - \beta H}}$. Substituting $v$ and $c_0 = \alpha\sqrt{T_0}$:
$$ M = \frac{h \alpha\sqrt{T_0}}{\alpha\sqrt{T_0 - \beta H} \sqrt{\alpha^2 T_0 t^2 - h^2}} = \frac{h \sqrt{T_0}}{\sqrt{(T_0 - \beta H)(\alpha^2 T_0 t^2 - h^2)}} $$

**Part d**
The sonic boom will not be audible from the ground if the acoustic rays bend so much that they turn horizontal before reaching the ground, creating a shadow zone. A ray turns horizontal when its vertical component of velocity becomes zero, which occurs when the angle with the vertical is $90^\circ$. By Snell's law, $\sin\alpha(z) / c(z) = 1/v$, the ray turns horizontal at an altitude $z_t$ where $c(z_t) = v$. 
Since $c(z) = \alpha\sqrt{T_0 - \beta z}$ increases as $z$ decreases, the ray will not reach the ground if the speed of sound at the ground exceeds the plane's speed, i.e., $v < c(0)$. 
Thus, the condition for the boom to be inaudible is $v < \alpha\sqrt{T_0}$, which gives:
$$ M = \frac{v}{c(H)} < \frac{\alpha\sqrt{T_0}}{\alpha\sqrt{T_0 - \beta H}} = \sqrt{\frac{T_0}{T_0 - \beta H}} $$
Therefore, the upper limit for the Mach number for which this occurs is:
$$ M_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{T_0}{T_0 - \beta H}} $$

**Final Answers:**
a. A cone with half-angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, where $\sin\theta = 1/M$.
b. A horn-like or trumpet-shaped curved surface opening outwards (curving away from the vertical) as it extends downwards.
c. $M = \frac{h \sqrt{T_0}}{\sqrt{(T_0 - \beta H)(\alpha^2 T_0 t^2 - h^2)}}$
d. $M_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{T_0}{T_0 - \beta H}}$

**Problem B3: Locked and Moded**

a. Consider two mirrors facing each other separated by a distance $L$ (a Fabry–Pérot resonator). The cavity (the space between the two mirrors) is in vacuum (index of refraction $n = 1$, no dispersion), and the mirrors have high reflectivities so that the main resonance condition is that an integer multiple of half-wavelengths fit into the cavity. A light pulse containing multiple different frequencies travels between the mirrors and interferes with itself.
i. State the condition for resonance in terms of $L$ and wavelength $\lambda$.
ii. Write down an expression for the resonant angular frequencies $\omega_m$, with $m$ counting each of the possible resonances.
iii. What is the angular frequency spacing $\Delta\omega \equiv \omega_{m+1} - \omega_m$ between adjacent angular frequencies?

b. The electric field at the antinodes of the standing waves in the resonator is a superposition of oscillations at the resonant angular frequencies and is given by:
$$E_{\text{before}}(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{+\infty} E_k \cos[(k \Delta\omega) t]$$
Now suppose we introduce a gain medium (such as a doped crystal) into the laser cavity. The gain medium completely absorbs incoming light and re-emits it over a finite range of $N$ angular frequencies centered around some angular frequency $\omega_0$, which coincides with one of the $\omega_m$ values determined above. Within this bandwidth, the gain medium amplifies and supports oscillations at all $\omega_m$ that fall within the range. (Assume $N$ is an odd number.)
Assume that each of these $N$ angular frequencies—also referred to as modes—has the same amplitude $E_0$, and that their phases are locked such that there is zero relative phase between them at $t = 0$. This condition is known as mode locking. Set their common phase so that all electric fields are expressed as cosine functions, consistent with the form of $E_{\text{before}}(t)$.
i. Write an expression for the total electric field $E_{\text{after}}(t)$ as the sum of these $N$ equally spaced angular frequencies (with zero relative phase).
ii. Show that in the limit of many angular frequencies ($\Delta\omega \ll \omega_0$, $N \gg 1$), the time-dependent electric field approximately takes the following form:
$$E_{\text{after}}(t) \approx E_0 f(\omega_0, t) \frac{\sin\left(\frac{N (\Delta\omega) t}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{(\Delta\omega) t}{2}\right)}$$
and determine the function $f(\omega_0, t)$.

c. To answer the next part of the problem, assume $N$ is odd and find the following limit when $a = \pi m$, where $m$ is an integer:
$$\lim_{x \to a} \frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}$$

d. Mode locking can dramatically increase the peak intensity $I$ of the laser output. Use the expression $I = \gamma E^2$, where $\gamma$ is a known constant, to answer the following questions.
i. Determine the total instantaneous intensity $I_{\text{after}}(t)$ of the electric field.
